reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: A constellation of multiple left-heart obstructive lesions arranged in series along the inflow and outflow of the left ventricle
The classic four components are a supravalvar mitral ring, parachute mitral valve, subaortic stenosis and coarctation of the aorta
Incomplete forms with two or three components are common, and lesions may be at valvar, subvalvar or supravalvar level
Obstruction at several levels compounds the load on the left heart and drives pulmonary venous hypertension
Presentation depends on the dominant and most severe lesion, ranging from a critically ill neonate with coarctation to an older child with exertional symptoms
A thorough echocardiographic survey is essential because a single obvious lesion may distract from additional serial obstructions
Management is staged surgical or catheter relief of each significant obstruction, with the mitral apparatus often the most challenging to address
reference.pathophysiology: Shone complex is a spectrum of developmental left-heart obstructions occurring in series, so that blood entering and leaving the left ventricle meets resistance at multiple levels. A supravalvar mitral ring and a parachute mitral valve (chordae inserting into a single papillary muscle) impede left atrial emptying and mimic mitral stenosis, raising pulmonary venous pressure. Subaortic and aortic obstruction, together with coarctation, impede left ventricular ejection and impose pressure loading. Because the obstructions are additive, even individually mild lesions can combine to produce significant pulmonary venous hypertension, left atrial and pulmonary vascular changes, and impaired systemic output. The neonatal coarctation component may render the systemic circulation duct-dependent.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated subaortic or valvar aortic stenosis
additionalInvestigations: Comprehensive transthoracic echocardiography to map every level of left-heart obstruction
Doppler gradients across the mitral apparatus, subaortic region, aortic valve and aortic arch
Cardiac MR or CT angiography to define arch anatomy and coarctation
Cardiac catheterisation to assess pulmonary vascular resistance and residual gradients
Chest radiograph and electrocardiogram for chamber enlargement and pulmonary congestion
Serial imaging to track progression of individual lesions over time
redFlags: Neonatal circulatory collapse from a duct-dependent coarctation component
Severe pulmonary venous hypertension or pulmonary oedema
Rising left atrial pressure with a restrictive mitral apparatus
Progressive left ventricular dysfunction from combined obstructions
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the number and severity of lesions and especially on the mitral valve, which is difficult to repair and prone to residual stenosis; multilevel and mitral-dominant disease carries a guarded prognosis and often needs repeated intervention.
pitfalls: Relieving one obvious obstruction while overlooking additional serial lesions that limit benefit
Underestimating the mitral component, which frequently dictates long-term outcome
Assuming an isolated coarctation and missing the wider complex
Failing to reassess for progression of previously mild lesions after intervention
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
